\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{ङ} (ṅa)}{ङ (ṅa)}]{\sk{ङ} (ṅa) — the nasal before \sk{ख} in \sk{सङ्ख्या}}

\label{lesson:SA-W65-letter-nga}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \sk{इ} and \sk{ऋ} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\sk{सङ्ख्या}} (\emph{saṅkhyā}), \textquotedblleft{}number\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ङ}}
\textbf{\sk{ङ}} — \emph{ṅa}, the nasal made where \emph{k} and \emph{kh} are made.

It is inside \textbf{\sk{सङ्ख्या}} (\emph{saṅkhyā}), \textquotedblleft{}number\textquotedblright{}, from the chapter on numbers. Say \emph{saṅkhyā}: the \emph{ṅ} sits at the back of the mouth, ready for the \emph{kh} after it. Sanskrit spells that nasal out as \textbf{\sk{ङ}}; Hindi writes the same word \textbf{\sk{संख्या}}, with a dot above instead.

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ङ}}
Put your pen on \sk{ङ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start this letter or which way to travel}. It is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\sk{सङ्ख्या}} and point at \sk{ङ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ङ} three times, saying \emph{ṅ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \sk{ऋ}, then \sk{ङ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{सङ्ख्या}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \sk{ङ}? (\textbf{ṅa}, \emph{ṅ}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\sk{सङ्ख्या}}, \emph{saṅkhyā}, \textquotedblleft{}number\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} … (namaste. ahaṁ …)}{नमस्ते। अहं संस्कृतं … (namaste. ahaṁ …)}]{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि।} — two known sentences, one tiny text}

\label{lesson:SA-W65-connected-text-guided-copy}



\begin{quote}
Read the whole text once: \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि।}} It says only two things you already know: “Hello. I speak Sanskrit.” Every word, sign, conjunct, and danda has already been taught. There is no new vocabulary here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy of connected text}
Keep the model visible. Copy \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते।}} once. Leave one clear word space, then copy \textbf{\sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि।}} Read each word as your hand reaches it.

Copy the complete two-sentence text once more on a fresh line:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि।}}
\end{quote}

Check the two danda marks, the space after the first one, both anusvāra dots, the vocalic-ṛ sign in \textbf{\sk{संस्कृतं}}, and the joined \textbf{\sk{स्त}} inside \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते}}. Credit requires the connected Devanagari text; romanization is not an answer.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many sentences and how many danda marks did you write? (\textbf{Two and two.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} … (namaste. ahaṁ …)}{नमस्ते। अहं संस्कृतं … (namaste. ahaṁ …)}]{Two sentences after the model closes}

\label{lesson:SA-W65-connected-text-delayed-copy}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि।}} once. Say its two meanings: “Hello. I speak Sanskrit.” Notice where each sentence ends.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy of the whole text}
Cover the model now. Wait ten seconds without writing. Then write both sentences from memory, with a danda after each one. There is no visible answer and no romanization while you write.

Uncover and compare only after one complete attempt:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि।}}
\end{quote}

Check in this order: two complete sentences; two danda marks; word spaces; both anusvāra dots; \textbf{\sk{◌ृ}}; joined \textbf{\sk{स्त}}. Repair only the first difference, then read the repaired text aloud. A Latin-letter version earns no Devanagari writing credit.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What support disappeared? (\textbf{The visible model; the meaning and the text stayed the same.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} … (namaste. ahaṁ …)}{नमस्ते। अहं संस्कृतं … (namaste. ahaṁ …)}]{Meanings only — recall the complete Devanagari text}

\label{lesson:SA-W65-connected-text-independent-recall}



\begin{quote}
Put every Sanskrit model away. The prompt below gives meanings only. Nothing new is being composed or translated: these are the same two old sentences in the same order.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — independent connected-text recall}
Write in Devanagari:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item “Hello.” Literally, “a bow to you.”
  \item “I speak Sanskrit.”
\end{enumerate}

Put a danda after each sentence. Stop after one complete attempt; do not use a visible Devanagari model or a romanized cue.

Now uncover the answer: \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते।} \sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि।}} Award credit only if both known sentences are complete, ordered, separated, and closed with danda marks in Devanagari. Romanization earns no credit. If one feature differs, repair that feature and write the whole two-sentence text once more from memory.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The runway began with one traced \textbf{\sk{न}}. What can you now produce without a model? (\textbf{A complete two-sentence Devanagari text from meaning alone.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(controlled location question)]{Your first question from meaning}

\label{lesson:SA-W65-kutra-controlled-question}



\begin{quote}
Close the earlier lessons. Recall \textbf{book}, \textbf{where?}, and \textbf{is} without writing any of them yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing: assemble one familiar question}
From meaning alone, write \textbf{Where is the book?} There is no word bank, romanization, or copyable sentence. Choose the three familiar pieces, put them in a clear Sanskrit order, and add the question mark. This composition is untimed: finish before opening the answer key.

\subsection*{Your turn: repair one difference}
Check the thing, place question, copula, word boundaries, and punctuation separately. Repair the first difference and write the whole question once more from meaning.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What made this composition rather than copying? (\textbf{You selected and ordered three known pieces from meaning, with no visible Sanskrit answer.})

One controlled line proves this rung, not the later timed A1 writing task.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(short timed A1 writing checkpoint)]{A short A1 writing checkpoint}

\label{lesson:SA-W65-a1-timed-production}



\begin{quote}
This is a short independent attempt, not a model. You will write the answers, and this page will not show you any copyable Sanskrit answer.

Put away romanization, dictionaries, translators, and spell-checkers. Keep a blank page ready and set a \textbf{three-minute timer}. Write in Devanagari. Ordinary legible handwriting is enough; decorative calligraphy is not scored.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — timed assessment production}
\textbf{One practical form — three minutes}

Complete \textbf{all six fields in Devanagari} for a new neighbourhood activity group. Short answers are enough. Start the timer when you begin the first field; leave any unfinished field as evidence when it rings.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Your name
  \item Where you live or stay
  \item A language you speak
  \item One everyday action or kind of work you do
  \item One drink or food you like
  \item One person in your family
\end{enumerate}

When the three-minute timer rings, \textbf{stop}. Record the number of completed fields. An honest short attempt is more useful than a perfect untimed one.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Spend at most one minute looking at this first attempt. Note one field you completed clearly and one field to practise next; do not rewrite the timed answer. Keep the page as evidence.

This checkpoint is \textbf{not} the complete A1 writing paper. On another day, close this lesson and open the separate \href{https://github.com/adhithyan15/coding-adventures/blob/main/code/learning/human-languages/sanskrit/mocks/a1/mock-1.md}{A1 mock 1 learner paper} for the authentic form and named-reader message under one 20-minute assessment clock. That paper and its later rubric review are a separate assessment session, not work inside this four-minute lesson. The second mock is a separate repeat, not a model to copy.
\end{tcolorbox}
